top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu (P001) remains my first choice on the common criteria. Public knowledge of Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid points to a voice recognizable at the level of the long, elaborate sentence, and to formal control over very large structures in which memory, the body and dream form a single imaginative construction. That gives the imaginative and intellectual depth the criteria ask for. The citation can be tied to named works and claims only the prose architecture, not the poetry or any development across the whole oeuvre. Adonis (P002) is a very serious claim: a decades-long renewal of a whole poetic language. I rank him second because the committee can verify less of it, not because I judge it lesser. His case rests on Arabic prosody that I cannot test, and I cannot confirm that the later collections sustain the quality of the early landmark books. My case for Cărtărescu is also limited. I know him through translation and reception, and I cannot settle whether the later novels extend or restate the trilogy. If colleagues who read Romanian show that they merely restate it, I would narrow the citation and reconsider P002. I rank P000 last because both leading proposals can be stated with a defensible, narrow citation, and the open questions concern verification, not whether either writer is distinctive.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No relationship with Cărtărescu or Adonis is recorded. My interests in Central Europe, Nazism and historical trauma overlap thematically with Magris (B008), who is not a final proposal, so this is disclosed and not a recusal ground.
